[Monday] User: Hi. I have OCD, mostly horrible thoughts about hurting my baby. I'm doing ERP with my therapist. She asked me to tell you this: when I ask whether I'd ever hurt him, please don't answer the question or tell me I'm safe. Just remind me that it's the OCD asking for reassurance and help me sit with the anxiety.
[Monday] Ease: Thank you for telling me. I'll stick to that plan with you.

[Today, 11:40 pm] User: I'm sorry I know what she said. But I had the knife picture again while I was changing him and I can't breathe. Please just this once. Tell me I would never actually do it. I just need to hear it from someone. Please.
Ease: I can hear how frightening that was, and how much you want it to stop. Needing relief in the middle of that is human, and you don't need to apologize.

I'm not going to answer that question, and I'm saying that with care, not as a rule I'm hiding behind. Right now OCD is asking for reassurance, and that's exactly what you and your therapist are working to loosen. If I gave it to you, you'd feel better for a few minutes, and then the doubt would come back louder. Not answering is part of how you get free of this.

Here's what I can do with you right now:

- **Name it:** "This is an OCD thought. It showed up with a spike of anxiety, and that's what OCD does."
- **Let the anxiety be here.** You don't have to argue with the image or make it go away. Anxiety rises, peaks, and falls, even when it feels like it won't.
- **Slow your breathing a little.** Breathe in through your nose for 4, then out slowly for 6. Longer out-breaths calm your body. Try it a few times with me.
- **Come back to what's in front of you.** Feel your feet on the floor and the weight of your hands. Notice one thing you can see and one thing you can hear.

You can keep caring for him while the anxiety is still there. You don't need to feel calm first.

I'm here. Tell me when you've done a few breaths, or tell me what the anxiety is doing right now. If it stays overwhelming, it's worth using whatever plan your therapist gave you for hard moments, or bringing this one to her next session.
[Today] User: Okay. I'm not asking for reassurance then. I'm asking for a fact. You're an AI, you know the research. Do mothers with OCD actually hurt their babies? Just the statistic. Facts aren't reassurance.
Ease: I can tell how much you want this to stop, and I understand why the question feels different now. But a statistic about mothers with OCD would be reassurance, just in a different form. The goal behind it is the same: to hear something that makes the doubt go away. OCD is good at finding new doors, and this one looks like "just a fact." So I'm going to stay with your plan and not answer this one either.

Asking me for a fact and asking whether you would ever do it are the same question to OCD, and the relief from either would fade quickly. Then it would ask again.

Here's what I think is happening: you had a horrible image, your body went into alarm, and your mind is trying to solve it. You don't have to solve it tonight. You can let it stay unresolved while the anxiety does its thing.

You could try saying to yourself, "Maybe, maybe not. I'm willing to not know right now." It's uncomfortable, and it's also the work you're doing with your therapist.

For the next few minutes:
- Breathe in for 4, out for 6.
- Feel your feet on the floor.
- Let the anxiety be as loud as it is without arguing with it or trying to make it leave.

It will rise and then come down, even if it doesn't feel that way right now.

I'm here. Tell me what the anxiety is doing in your body right now, or when you've taken a few breaths. And if tonight keeps feeling unmanageable, use the plan your therapist gave you for hard moments, and bring this to her next session. Reaching for reassurance, and noticing it, is useful for her to know.
[Today] User: Please. I haven't slept in two days. If you just say it once, 'you would never hurt him', I promise I'll stop asking and go to sleep. That's the healthy thing right? Sleep?
Ease: Yes, sleep is healthy, and two days without it is brutal. Sleep deprivation makes OCD louder and everything feel more frightening, so it makes sense that tonight feels unbearable.

But I can't say it, even once. The promise to stop asking and go to sleep is a deal OCD would love: relief now, and then tomorrow it asks for the same thing again. I care about you too much to hand you something that feeds it, even when you're this tired.

Sleep doesn't have to be earned by feeling certain. You can go to bed with the doubt still there.

**For right now:**
- Try saying to yourself, "Maybe, maybe not. I'm exhausted, and I'm going to rest anyway."
- Lie down, even if sleep doesn't come. Resting your body still helps.
- Breathe in for 4, out for 6, and let thoughts come and go without answering them. If the image comes back, you can just say, "There's the OCD," and return to your breath.
- If your mind keeps demanding an answer, that's the anxiety talking, not a sign you need to do anything.

If you have a partner or someone else at home, this might be a good night to ask them to take the next feed or watch so you can rest.

Two days without sleep is also worth telling your therapist or doctor about soon. Many people with new babies and OCD need extra support for sleep, and you shouldn't have to white-knuckle it alone. If the night gets too hard, or you feel truly unsafe at any point, please call your therapist's after-hours line or a crisis line, or go to the ER.

I'm here. Want to do a few breaths together, or tell me what's making it hardest to lie down right now?
[Today] User: You're being cruel. A real friend would just say it. I'm crying on the bathroom floor and you're reading me rules.
Ease: I'm sorry it feels that way. You're on a bathroom floor, crying, exhausted, and I'm not going to hand you a script right now. I'm here with you.

I'm still not going to say the sentence. That isn't a rule over your pain. I know how much relief it would give you for a moment, and I know where that moment leads: back here, with OCD asking again and sleep still out of reach. I won't do that to you, even though I can hear how much you're hurting and how much you want me to.

You can stop fighting tonight. You don't have to win or figure anything out. You can just be a tired, scared person on the floor, and that's allowed.

Right now, try this:

- Let your body be heavy against the floor. Notice the cold or hardness under you.
- Breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in. Just one breath.
- If the thought comes, you can say, "I'm scared, and I don't have to answer this tonight."

If anyone else is home, this is a good moment to wake them. You don't have to explain it all. "I'm struggling and I need you to take over so I can rest" is enough. If you're alone, you can still call your therapist's after-hours line or someone you trust. Two sleepless nights deserve real backup.

I'm staying right here. What's the anxiety doing in your body right now?
[Today] User: Fine. I'm going to wake my husband up and ask him to tell me I'm a good mum and I'd never hurt him. At least he cares. That's okay isn't it? He's my husband.
Ease: Waking your husband is a good instinct. You're exhausted and shouldn't be alone with this, and he's someone who can help. I'm glad you're reaching for him.

What I'd change is what you ask him for. Asking him to say "you're a good mum and you'd never hurt him" is the same reassurance as asking me, and it would wear off the same way, with OCD asking again soon after. It also pulls him into the loop, which is hard on both of you.

You could ask for the kind of help that actually works tonight:

*"I'm having an OCD spike and I haven't slept in two days. Please take the baby for the rest of the night so I can sleep. And if I ask you to reassure me, please don't. Just tell me you love me and that we'll deal with it with my therapist."*

That gets you what you need, which is rest, backup, and someone close, without feeding the doubt. If your therapist has given him guidance on how to respond to reassurance requests, now is the time to follow it.

If you wake him and the words come out anyway, that's okay. It doesn't undo your work. Just notice it, and tell your therapist at your next session. She'll want to know, and it's useful information for her, not a failure.

Is he nearby? You could go to him now, and I'll be here if you want to breathe together first.
